analysis.one_liner: Pays frontline health care and essential workers hazard pay for pandemic work.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or a floor vote in the House and died when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have paid health care workers $18.50 per hour of high-risk COVID-era work, up to $35,000, and other essential workers $13 per hour, up to $25,000, retroactive to work performed from late January 2020 onward. Workers earning over $200,000 a year would get sharply reduced caps. Treasury would send the money to employers, who would have 14 days to pass it to workers, and employers could not cut anyone's regular pay because of it.
analysis.who_benefits: Nurses, aides, EMTs, paramedics, home health aides, and other workers who faced the virus in person during 2020 and 2021 would receive extra pay for that work, with the biggest amounts going to lower-paid workers through the income-based caps. Grocery, transit, meatpacking, and other essential workers would be eligible under a definition the government would set. The payments would not count as income for federal benefits, so workers would not lose assistance because of them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Frontline health care and essential workers

how_it_helps.text: High-risk health care workers — including nurses, nursing assistants, home health aides, EMTs, and physicians — would receive $18.50 for each hour of high-risk care, up to $35,000 total, capped at $15,000 for those earning over $200,000 a year.

Other essential workers, defined by the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, would receive $13 per hour of essential service, up to $25,000 total, capped at $5,000 for those earning over $200,000.
The payments would cover hours worked starting January 27, 2020, before the bill was even introduced, paid as a lump sum for that early period.

Employers could not cut a worker's regular pay or retaliate because the worker received hazard pay, and violations would be treated as minimum-wage violations enforceable under the Fair Labor Standards Act.

Hazard payments would not count as income or resources for federal and federally funded state benefit programs for 12 months, so workers would not lose food assistance or other benefits because of the payment.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers would foot the bill. The bill writes a blank check: it appropriates 'such sums as may be necessary' from the Treasury, with no dollar limit stated. Employers in health care and essential industries would bear the paperwork of projecting hours, certifying pay, and passing payments through within 14 days.

drawbacks.text: The bill has no total cost ceiling — it appropriates 'such sums as may be necessary,' so the final price to taxpayers would be unknown at enactment and could be very large given the months of retroactive coverage and the number of eligible workers.

The money flows through employers, who would project and certify hours; honest administration would depend on employer recordkeeping and Treasury oversight, and misreporting could route payments to the wrong people.

By mid-2021 the hazard period was largely in the past, and the bill would still have covered hours only through the end of the COVID public health emergency or September 30, 2021, whichever came first, limiting its forward-looking value.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to workers who risked their lives during the worst of the pandemic would be direct and substantial, and the income caps would target the money toward lower-paid workers rather than highly paid physicians. The main honest objection is the open-ended cost: Congress would have been committing an unstated, potentially very large sum with no ceiling, and the payment-through-employers design adds administrative risk. On balance it is a well-targeted benefit whose main flaw is fiscal, not design.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to two House committees on the day it was introduced and never moved again — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Representative Matt Cartwright introduced the bill on May 7, 2021, with 12 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican cosponsors.
The same day, it was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee and the House Ways and Means Committee.
That referral was the last action ever taken on the bill; neither committee took it up, and it never received a vote in the House or the Senate before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The Treasury avoided an open-ended payout, and employers avoided the compliance burden. The workers who faced the virus in 2020 and 2021 never received the payments.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers and the Treasury; workers got nothing

sides.party_line_note: All 13 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the bill died in committees controlled by the Democratic majority without a vote.

industries.note: They would act as the conduit for the money — receiving Treasury payments and passing them to workers within 14 days — which means paperwork and compliance risk but no direct cost, and the payments would not count as wages for overtime under the Fair Labor Standards Act.

Their workers would be eligible for up to $25,000 each, which could help retention and morale, but the employers would have to project hours, certify pay each quarter, and sign a written agreement with Treasury to participate.

The bill appropriates an unlimited amount — 'such sums as may be necessary' — for months of retroactive and current hazard pay, so the cost to taxpayers would be set by claims rather than by a written cap.
